29 A parallel beam of white light passes through a diffraction grating. Orange light of wavelength
600 nm in the fourth-order diffraction maximum coincides with blue light in the fifth-order
diffraction maximum.
What is the wavelength of the blue light?
A
450 nm
B
480 nm
C
500 nm
D
750 nm

hints: Notice the word coincides for the $600\text{ nm}$ fourth order and the blue fifth order - it means both colours diffract at the same angle $\theta$ through the same grating.
Recall the grating equation $d\sin\theta = n\lambda$ with the same $d$ and same $\sin\theta$ for the two overlapping maxima.
Set $4 \times 600\text{ nm}$ equal to $5 \times \lambda_{blue}$ and solve for $\lambda_{blue}$, checking it is shorter than $600\text{ nm}$.
walkthrough: Identify the given data: orange $\lambda_o = 600\text{ nm}$ with order $n_o = 4$, and blue $\lambda_b = ?$ with order $n_b = 5$, both at the same diffracted angle $\theta$.
State the governing rule: for a diffraction grating $d\sin\theta = n\lambda$, where $d$ is the grating spacing.
Because $d$ and $\theta$ are the same for the coincident maxima, $d\sin\theta$ is common, so $n_o\lambda_o = n_b\lambda_b$.
Substitute values with units: $4 \times 600\text{ nm} = 5 \times \lambda_b$, so $2400\text{ nm} = 5\lambda_b$.
Divide to find $\lambda_b = 2400/5\text{ nm} = 480\text{ nm}$, which is sensibly shorter than orange light for a higher order at the same angle. This is option B.

A.explanation: Gives $450\text{ nm}$, which would require $4 \times 600 = 5 \times 450$ to hold, but $2400 \ne 2250$.

B.explanation: Satisfies $4 \times 600\text{ nm} = 5 \times 480\text{ nm}$ for the same $d\sin\theta$, so the two maxima coincide.

C.explanation: Gives $500\text{ nm}$, which confuses the ratio and does not satisfy $4 \times 600\text{ nm} = 5\lambda$.

D.explanation: Gives $750\text{ nm}$, larger than orange light, whereas fifth order at the same angle must have a shorter wavelength than fourth order.
